confidenceTitle: Confidence through knowing who we are
confidenceIntro: The Creator is our shared identity, rather than a distant power before which we are small. Recognising who we are brings natural confidence and inner strength into ordinary life.
confidenceIdentity: A personality may feel small beside another person’s wealth, authority, or approval. Look deeper into who you are: if we are the shared Creator, possessions and status are merely parts of the creation, not measures of our worth. This shared identity belongs equally to the person who disagrees with you; it gives no one superiority.
confidenceExample: Suppose you are rejected for a job and think, “I am worth less than everyone else.” In this teaching, rejection belongs to a role within the game, not the whole of your identity. Remembering the shared Creator can make room to learn, ask for feedback, and apply again. Preparation and effort remain part of the unfolding, even though you cannot guarantee the next result.
confidenceEnquiry: Two questions invite sincere self-enquiry: how does this shared identity resonate with your experience, and what changes when you meet life this way? Knowing who you are brings grounded confidence and less dependence on external approval. You are free to explore at your own pace; a challenging day does not make you a failure.
confidenceReflection: When you compare yourself with someone, what makes you feel smaller? What does the shared Creator mean to you in that scene? Examine both the idea and any change you actually notice, without requiring yourself to agree.
enjoyment: Recognition does not end enjoyment—it deepens it exponentially. A leaf, a tree, a flower, a quiet conversation, or the morning sky becomes breathtaking when experienced as our shared creation. Laughter, sorrow, love, and compassion coexist with unshakable inner steadiness. Understanding who we are enriches every moment of this game.
familyTitle: Protection, patience, and openness to correction
familyMoney: If someone takes shared family money without permission, remember the same Creator in both lives while protecting the money and restricting access. Ask what is happening: an unmet need and the financing of harmful activity call for different responses. Care can include practical help, firm boundaries, and appropriate lawful action. Recognition does not require leaving others exposed to harm.
familyRecovery: When a family faces a loss, the focus should be on helping people settle and working towards recovery without blame or humiliation. Offer room to heal and change where possible. Support and recovery take time. The same shared identity also includes someone who offers you valid correction: listen with humility, check the truth, and adjust your course with grace.
familyReflection: What needs protection in this scene? Can you recognise the same source while setting a boundary, allowing room for change, or accepting a valid correction?
traditionIntro: This teaching is a modern clarification of the timeless truth discovered through thousands of years of meditative enquiry, rather than a new religion. Earlier seers and traditions can be studied respectfully, honoring their original context and profound insights.
ramana: Ramana Maharshi’s Who Am I? directs enquiry towards the source of the sense of “I”, rather than identification with the body or thinking mind. This offers a point of comparison with our invitation to investigate identity. It does not by itself establish our account of a game designed before entry.
vivekananda: In Soul, Nature and God, Vivekananda describes the Advaita conclusion of one infinite soul appearing as many. This can be compared with our shared-source explanation. The lecture also distinguishes philosophical positions; it should not be read as saying that all traditions agree on creation, rebirth, or the design of events.
